scenes.narration: The self that experiences Unforgiven is a committee, not a king. Unforgiven is a 1992 American revisionist Western film produced and directed by Clint Eastwood from a screenplay by David Webb Peoples. It stars Eastwood as William Munny, an aging outlaw and killer who takes on one more job years after he turned to farming.

Reproduction explains more of Unforgiven than any philosophy dares to admit. Unforgiven premiered at the Mann Bruin Theater on August 3, 1992, before being released by Warner Bros. on August 7, 1992. It grossed over $159 million on a budget of $14.4 million and received widespread critical acclaim, with praise for the acting (particularly from Eastwood and Hackman), directing, editing, themes, and cinematography.

Once you see Unforgiven as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. The film won four Academy Awards: Best Picture, Best Director for Eastwood, Best Supporting Actor for Hackman, and Best Film Editing for Joel Cox. Eastwood was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Actor for his performance, but lost to Al Pacino for Scent of a Woman.

The story Unforgiven tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. The film was the third Western to win Best Picture, following Cimarron (1931) and Dances With Wolves (1990). Eastwood dedicated the film to directors and mentors Sergio Leone and Don Siegel.

Meaning is not found in Unforgiven — it is manufactured for it. In 2004, Unforgiven was selected for preservation in the United States National Film Registry by the Library of Congress as being deemed "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant". In 1880, in the fictional town of Big Whiskey, Wyoming, a cowboy named Quick Mike slashes prostitute Delilah Fitzgerald's face with a knife over an insult, permanently disfiguring her.

The cold light on Unforgiven leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. As punishment, Sheriff "Little Bill" Daggett orders Mike and his associate who was with him at the brothel, Davey Bunting, to turn over several of their ponies to Delilah's employer, Skinny DuBois, for his loss of revenue. In Hodgeman County, Kansas, a boastful young man visits Will Munny's hog farm.

Unforgiven did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. He calls himself the "Schofield Kid" and claims to be an experienced bounty hunter looking for help pursuing the cowboys. Formerly a notorious outlaw and murderer, Will is now a repentant widower raising two children.

The honest version of Unforgiven starts by giving up the comforting part. After initially refusing to help, Will realizes that his farm is failing and his children's future is in jeopardy. He recruits his friend Ned Logan, another retired outlaw, and they catch up with the Kid, who they discover is severely near-sighted.

Strip Unforgiven of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. Back in Big Whiskey, British-born gunfighter "English" Bob, an old acquaintance and rival of Little Bill's, arrives in town with his biographer W.W. Enforcing the town's antigun law, Little Bill, with his deputies, disarms Bob and beats him savagely to discourage others from attempting to claim the bounty.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Unforgiven shows exactly where that breaks. Bob, humiliated, is banished from town the next morning, but Beauchamp stays out of a fascination with the sheriff, who debunks many of the romantic notions Beauchamp has about the Wild West. Little Bill explains to Beauchamp that the best attribute for a gunslinger is to be cool-headed under fire rather than to have the quickest draw, and to always kill the best shooter first.

What looks like free choice in Unforgiven is older than choice itself. Will, Ned, and the Kid arrive in town during a rainstorm and enter Skinny's saloon. While Ned and the Kid meet with the prostitutes upstairs, Little Bill confronts a feverish Will.

Nobody designed the part of Unforgiven you experience — it was inherited. Not realizing Will's identity, but correctly guessing that he wants the bounty, Bill confiscates his weapon and beats him. Ned and the Kid escape through a back window and take Will to an unoccupied barn outside of town, where they and the prostitutes nurse him back to health.

Every serious account of Unforgiven eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. After missing Davey and shooting his horse, Ned falters and Will shoots Davey instead. Ned is later captured and flogged to death by Little Bill to learn the whereabouts of Will and the Kid.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Unforgiven — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. Will takes the Kid with him to the cowboys' ranch, directing him to ambush Quick Mike in the outhouse and shoot him. After they escape, a distraught Kid drunkenly confesses he had never killed anyone before.

The selfish-gene reading of Unforgiven makes it less romantic and far more precise. Little Sue arrives with the reward and tells them about Ned's fate. Shocked by the news, Will begins drinking and demands the Kid's revolver.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. The Kid hands it over, saying that he no longer wants to be a killer, and Will sends him back to Kansas to distribute the reward. That night Will finds Ned's corpse displayed in a coffin outside Skinny's saloon.

The feeling that Unforgiven means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. Will walks in brandishing a shotgun and kills Skinny for displaying Ned's corpse. In the ensuing gunfight, Will shoots Little Bill and several other members of the posse with the revolver.

Nothing in Unforgiven was built for you — it was built for reproduction. Little Bill tries and fails to take another shot at Will while lying on the floor, then bemoans his fate and curses Will, who shoots him dead. Will shouts threats as he mounts his horse and rides out of town.

The psychology underneath Unforgiven is simpler and older than the story on top. A closing title card states that Will's mother-in-law found his farm abandoned years later, Will having possibly moved to San Francisco with the children. She remained at a loss to understand why her daughter married such a notorious outlaw and murderer.

Behind Unforgiven sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. The film was written by David Webb Peoples, who had written the Oscar-nominated film The Day After Trinity and co-written Blade Runner with Hampton Fancher. The concept for the film dated to 1976, when it was developed under the titles The Cut-Whore Killings and The William Munny Killings.

The nihilist does not deny Unforgiven — he only refuses to flatter it. The script was originally optioned by Francis Ford Coppola, who failed to raise the money to develop the project any further. By Eastwood's own recollection, he was given the script in the "early 80s", although he did not immediately pursue it, because according to him, "I thought I should do some other things first".

What culture calls destiny in Unforgiven is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. In 1984, Sonia Chernus, Eastwood's long-time story editor at Malpaso Productions, sent him a scathing memo after reading the script stating that "it doesn't deserve my time or yours" and is "an insult to this company" and that Eastwood should "get rid of it FAST". Eastwood personally phoned Harris to offer him the role of English Bob, and later said Harris was watching Eastwood's 1973 movie High Plains Drifter at the time of the phone call, leading to Harris thinking it was a prank.

The genes do not care about Unforgiven; they care about copies. Gene Hackman was hesitant to play Bill Daggett, as his daughters were upset that he was starring in too many violent films, but his agent and Eastwood convinced him to do it. Much of the film was shot in Alberta in August 1991 by director of photography Jack Green.

Take away the meaning and Unforgiven still functions — that is the disturbing part. Production designer Henry Bumstead, who had worked with Eastwood on High Plains Drifter, was hired to create the "drained, wintry look" of the Western. The railroad scenes were filmed on the Sierra Railroad in Tuolumne County, California.

The unconscious does not argue with Unforgiven; it simply acts first. Men who claim to be fearless killers are variously exposed as being either cowards, weaklings, or self-promoting liars, while others find that they no longer have it in them to take yet another life. A writer with no concept of the harshness and cruelty of frontier life publishes stories which glorify common criminals as infallible men of honor.

Unforgiven feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. Its earnings of $15 million ($7,252 average from 2,071 theaters) in its opening weekend was the best-ever opening for a Clint Eastwood film at that time. This was also the highest August opening weekend, holding that record until it was surpassed a year later by The Fugitive.

The bleak reading of Unforgiven is also the most testable one. The film closed on July 15, 1993, having spent nearly a full year in theaters (343 days / 49 weeks), having earned $101 million in North America, and another $58 million internationally for a total of $159 million worldwide. Review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes reports an approval rating of 96% based on 109 reviews, and an average rating of 8.80/10.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Unforgiven. Audiences polled by CinemaScore gave the film an average grade of "B+" on an A+ to F scale. Despite his initial reservations, Ebert eventually included the film in his "The Great Movies" list.
